NONPROFIT PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION MERGER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust · Acme Community Fund

RECITALS — MERGER OF A NONPROFIT PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION
Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust (each a constituent corporation) are considering a merger under California's Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, Chapter 10 (Mergers), Cal. Corp. Code §§ 6010-6022. Upon the merger becoming effective, Acme Community Fund will be the surviving corporation, and the separate existence of each other constituent corporation will cease. This information sheet describes the statutory merger procedure that applies specifically to a public benefit corporation — a separate, independently codified scheme from the General Corporation Law merger procedure (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1100-1113) that governs a merger between for-profit business corporations, and from the statutory conversion procedure that changes an entity's type rather than combining two or more entities. It records the statutory requirements and the approvals obtained for a proposed merger; it does not itself effect the merger of Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust or any other entity.

WHO A PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION MAY MERGE WITH FREELY, AND WHO REQUIRES THE ATTORNEY GENERAL'S CONSENT
California's public benefit corporation merger statute starts from a broad textual allowance — a public benefit corporation may merge with any domestic corporation, any foreign corporation, or any other business entity — but then narrows that allowance sharply. Without the Attorney General's prior written consent, a public benefit corporation may only actually merge with a limited, enumerated set of entities: another public benefit corporation, a religious corporation, a foreign nonprofit corporation, or an unincorporated association whose own governing documents irrevocably dedicate its assets to charitable, religious, or public purposes. A merger with any other kind of entity — including an ordinary for-profit business corporation — falls outside that free list and requires the Attorney General's prior written consent before it may proceed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A public benefit corporation may merge with any domestic corporation, foreign corporation (Section 171), or other business entity (Section 5063.5)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, general merger-partner allowance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6010.)
  "However, without the prior written consent of the Attorney General, a public benefit corporation may only merge with another public benefit corporation or a religious corporation or a foreign nonprofit corporation or an unincorporated association the governing documents of which provide that its assets are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the enumerated merger partners a public benefit corporation may merge with without the Attorney General's consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6010.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general rule and the enumerated exempt-merger-partner list; it does not reproduce the separate statutory definitions the section cross-references (Cal. Corp. Code § 171's definition of "foreign corporation" and § 5063.5's definition of "other business entity"), and it does not address the section's own further, narrower exemption for a public benefit corporation that is itself exempt from Attorney General supervision as a campaign-finance "committee" under Government Code §§ 12581, 12583, and 82013 merging with another similarly exempt public benefit corporation. The text quoted here is drawn from a single subdivision, § 6010(a); the two quotes below are two separate sentences from that same subdivision, not stitched from non-adjacent parts of the statute. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a public benefit corporation specifically — the parallel, separately numbered merger-partner rules for a mutual benefit corporation (Chapter 15, commencing with § 8010) and a religious corporation (which largely borrows this chapter by cross-reference, subject to its own carve-outs) are not addressed here. This document is informational only and does not determine whether the Attorney General's consent is or is not required for any specific proposed merger.

ADVANCE NOTICE TO THE ATTORNEY GENERAL, AND THE LIMIT ON WHAT A MEMBER MAY RECEIVE
Separate from the consent requirement for merging outside the enumerated partner list, California law imposes a notice duty that applies to every merger the statute allows: at least 20 days before the merger is consummated, the Attorney General must be given a copy of the proposed agreement of merger. The same section also limits what a member of a constituent corporation may receive when a merger of this kind occurs: without the Attorney General's prior written consent, a member may only receive or keep a membership in the surviving corporation, and only for or as a result of that member's membership in the constituent corporation — not some other form of payment or property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "At least 20 days prior to consummation of any merger allowed by subdivision (a), the Attorney General must be provided with a copy of the proposed agreement of merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(b), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, 20-day advance notice to the Attorney General (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6010.)
  "Without the prior written consent of the Attorney General, when a merger occurs pursuant to subdivision (a), each member of a constituent corporation may only receive or keep a membership in the surviving corporation for or as a result of the member’s membership in the constituent corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(c), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, limit on what a member may receive absent Attorney General consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6010.)
  Known gap: The 20-day advance-notice requirement is quoted here with internal whitespace normalized: the raw fetched HTML places a line-wrap (a literal newline and tab characters) between the words "proposed" and "agreement of merger," confirmed identical across two independent fetches using different User-Agent headers on 2026-09-08; the quote below collapses that whitespace to a single space without altering any word or punctuation. This section does not itself state what happens if the Attorney General objects during the 20-day window, or specify a required form or delivery method for the notice — the statute imposes a timing duty, not an approval or waiting-period mechanism, and this document does not address the Attorney General's own administrative practices (such as Registry of Charitable Trusts filing conventions) for handling that notice, which are not codified in this section. The membership-limit provision in subdivision (c) applies "when a merger occurs pursuant to subdivision (a)" — i.e., it is tied to the same merger-partner framework as the preceding clause in this document, not a freestanding rule.

BOARD APPROVAL AND REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE AGREEMENT OF MERGER
The board of each corporation that wants to merge must approve an agreement of merger. The constituent corporations are parties to that agreement, and other persons may be made parties to it as well. The statute specifies what the agreement must state: the terms and conditions of the merger; any amendments to the surviving corporation's articles that the merger will effect, including naming conventions if the surviving corporation takes a new name; any amendments to the surviving corporation's bylaws the merger will effect; the name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which one is the surviving corporation; the manner, if any, of converting memberships of the constituent corporations into memberships of the surviving corporation; and any other details or provisions the parties want to include.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The board of each corporation which desires to merge shall approve an agreement of merger. The constituent corporations shall be parties to the agreement of merger and other persons may be parties to the agreement of merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6011, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, board approval of the agreement of merger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6011.)
  "The agreement shall state:(a) The terms and conditions of the merger;(b) The amendments, subject to Sections 5810 and 5816, to the articles of the surviving corporation to be effected by the merger, if any; if any amendment changes the name of the surviving corporation, the new name may be the same as or similar to the name of a disappearing corporation, subject to subdivision (b) of Section 5122;(c) The amendments to the bylaws of the surviving corporation to be effected by the merger, if any;(d) The name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of the constituent corporations is the surviving corporation;(e) The manner, if any, of converting memberships of the constituent corporations into memberships of the surviving corporation; and(f) Such other details or provisions as are desired, if any."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6011, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, required contents of the agreement of merger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6011.)
  Known gap: This clause covers board approval and the required contents of the agreement itself; it does not address the separate member-approval requirement for the agreement's principal terms, which a companion clause in this document covers. It also does not reproduce the two cross-referenced statutes this section incorporates by reference — Cal. Corp. Code §§ 5810 and 5816, which govern what a public benefit corporation's articles may and may not provide, and constrain what article amendments a merger agreement may make, and § 5122(b), which conditions a surviving corporation's use of a disappearing corporation's name. Item (f) ("such other details or provisions as are desired") is an open-ended catch-all in the statute itself, not a specific requirement this document can enumerate further.

MEMBER APPROVAL OF THE PRINCIPAL TERMS OF THE MERGER
Beyond board approval, the principal terms of the merger must separately be approved by the members of each constituent corporation, and by any other person or persons whose approval of an articles amendment is required under that corporation's own articles. This member (or other-person) approval can be given either before or after the board's own approval — the statute does not fix a required sequence between the two.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The principal terms of the merger shall be approved by the members (Section 5034) of each constituent corporation and by each other person or persons whose approval of an amendment of articles is required by the articles; and the approval by the members (Section 5034) or such other person or persons required by this section may be given before or after the approval by the board."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6012, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, member approval of the merger's principal terms (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6012.)
  Known gap: This section defines "members" by cross-reference to Cal. Corp. Code § 5034, which this document does not reproduce; it also does not address how this approval requirement applies to a public benefit corporation that has no members at all, a structure California law separately permits for this corporation type. This document does not state what counts as the "principal terms" of a merger for purposes of triggering this approval requirement — that term is used but not separately defined in this section.

THE OFFICERS' CERTIFICATE, FILING, AND WHEN THE MERGER BECOMES EFFECTIVE
After the board and any required member approval, the surviving corporation must file a copy of the agreement of merger, together with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation, with the California Secretary of State. That certificate must state the total number of memberships of each class entitled to vote on the merger, identify any other person or persons whose approval was required, and state that the principal terms of the agreement were duly approved by the required vote of the members and, if applicable, by those other persons. The merger, and any amendment to the surviving corporation's articles contained in the agreement, becomes effective upon that filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "After approval of a merger by the board and any approval by the members (Section 5034) or other person or persons required by Section 6012, the surviving corporation shall file a copy of the agreement of merger with an officers’ certificate of each constituent corporation attached stating the total number of memberships of each class entitled to vote on the merger, identifying any other person or persons whose approval is required, and stating that the principal terms of the agreement in the form attached were duly approved by the required vote of the members and (if applicable) such other person or persons."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6014, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the officers' certificate and filing requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6014.)
  "The merger and any amendment of the articles of the surviving corporation contained in the merger agreement shall thereupon be effective (subject to subdivision (c) of Section 5008 and subject to the provisions of Section 6018) and the several parties thereto shall be one surviving corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6014, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, when the merger becomes effective (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6014.)
  Known gap: The effective-date rule quoted here is itself made subject to two other cross-referenced provisions this document does not detail: Cal. Corp. Code § 5008(c) and § 6018 (the latter addresses mergers involving a foreign corporation and can shift which jurisdiction's law governs the merger's mechanics and effective date when the surviving entity is foreign). This document also does not address the general instrument-filed-with-the-Secretary-of-State rule elsewhere in California corporate law that allows a delayed effective date of up to 90 days after filing — whether that general rule applies to a merger filed under this specific section was not independently verified for this document.

MERGING WITH A BUSINESS CORPORATION: WHICH STATUTES APPLY TO WHICH PARTY
California law separately addresses a merger between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation by specifying, for each type of constituent corporation, which statutory sections govern that constituent's side of the transaction. For a constituent public benefit corporation, Sections 6011, 6012, 6014, and 6015 apply; for a constituent mutual benefit corporation, Sections 8011, 8011.5, 8012, 8014, and 8015 apply; for a constituent religious corporation, Sections 6014 and 6015 and subdivisions (c) and (d) of Section 9640 apply; and for a constituent business corporation, Sections 1101, 1101.1, 1103, and 1104 (the General Corporation Law merger provisions) apply.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "If an agreement of merger is entered into between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation: (i) Sections 6011, 6012, 6014, and 6015 shall apply to any constituent public benefit corporation; (ii) Sections 8011, 8011.5, 8012, 8014, and 8015 shall apply to any constituent mutual benefit corporation; (iii) Sections 6014 and 6015 and subdivisions (c) and (d) of Section 9640 shall apply to any constituent religious corporation; and (iv) Sections 1101, 1101.1, 1103, and 1104 shall apply to any constituent business corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6019, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, applicable statutes for a merger between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6019.)
  Known gap: This cross-reference list is notable for what it does not include: it does not list Section 6010 — the section that otherwise requires the Attorney General's prior written consent for a public benefit corporation to merge with an entity outside the enumerated exempt list, and that requires 20 days' advance notice to the Attorney General — among the sections it says apply to a constituent public benefit corporation in this specific hybrid scenario. Because a business corporation is not one of the entity types Section 6010(a) exempts from the consent requirement, whether Section 6010's consent and notice duties nonetheless continue to apply to a public benefit corporation merging with a business corporation (as part of the same chapter's general framework) or whether this section's silence about 6010 has some narrower significance is a real textual question this document does not resolve; it was not able to locate secondary authority (case law or Attorney General guidance) addressing this specific cross-reference gap within the scope of this document's research. This document also does not address the Corporate Transparency Act, federal or California tax consequences, or securities-law implications of converting a nonprofit corporation's assets into a business corporation structure through this kind of merger.

EFFECT OF THE MERGER: SUCCESSOR LIABILITY AND PRESERVED CREDITOR RIGHTS
Once a merger under this chapter is effective, the separate existence of each disappearing party ceases, and the surviving party succeeds — without any separate transfer being needed — to all of the rights and property of each disappearing party. At the same time, the surviving party becomes subject to all of the debts and liabilities of each disappearing party, and to any trust obligations resting on a disappearing party's property, in the same manner as if the surviving party had incurred those obligations itself. The statute separately preserves all rights of creditors and all liens and trusts on or arising from a constituent corporation's property, though a lien or trust obligation on a disappearing party's property remains limited to the property it affected immediately before the merger's effective date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existences of the disappearing parties to the merger cease and the surviving party to the merger shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing parties to the merger and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each and trust obligations upon the property of a disappearing party in the same manner as if incurred by the surviving party to the merger."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6020(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, succession to rights, property, debts, and liabilities on merger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6020.)
  "All rights of creditors and all liens and trusts upon or arising from the property of each of the constituent corporations and other parties to the merger shall be preserved unimpaired, provided that the liens and trust obligations upon property of a disappearing party shall be limited to the property affected thereby immediately prior to the time the merger is effective."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6020(b), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, preservation of creditors' rights, liens, and trusts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6020.)
  Known gap: This section does not itself define what makes property subject to a "trust obligation" for these purposes — that determination (for example, whether a donor-restricted or dedicated-purpose asset is impressed with such an obligation) depends on separate California charitable-trust and cy pres doctrine that this document does not address. This document also does not quote subdivision (c) of this section, which addresses pending litigation continuing against the surviving party; the raw fetched HTML contains a stray double space at one point in that subdivision ("the surviving  party"), confirmed identical across two independent fetches on 2026-09-08, and this document omits a direct quotation of that subdivision rather than reproduce the anomaly.

RECORD OF APPROVALS OBTAINED
The undersigned record, for Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust, that the board of each constituent corporation approved the agreement of merger on September 5, 2026, and that the members (or other persons whose approval was required) approved the agreement's principal terms on September 10, 2026 as follows: approved by unanimous written consent of the members entitled to vote.

If notice to the California Attorney General was required under Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(b), that notice, together with a copy of the proposed agreement of merger, was provided on August 10, 2026.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: September 12, 2026

Jordan Lee, President

It does not itself effect the merger of Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust into Acme Community Fund or any other entity, is not the Secretary of State's official filing of the agreement of merger or the officers' certificate required by Cal. Corp. Code § 6014, and does not determine whether the Attorney General's consent is required for this particular merger. The current official forms and instructions are published by the California Secretary of State and the California Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts.]

Because a business corporation is not one of the entity types Section 6010(a) exempts from the consent requirement, whether Section 6010's consent and notice duties nonetheless continue to apply to a public benefit corporation merging with a business corporation (as part of the same chapter's general framework) or whether this section's silence about 6010 has some narrower significance is a real textual question this document does not resolve; it was not able to locate secondary authority (case law or Attorney General guidance) addressing this specific cross-reference gap within the scope of this document's research. This document also does not address the Corporate Transparency Act, federal or California tax consequences, or securities-law implications of converting a nonprofit corporation's assets into a business corporation structure through this kind of merger.

expectedJSON.body: Once a merger under this chapter is effective, the separate existence of each disappearing party ceases, and the surviving party succeeds — without any separate transfer being needed — to all of the rights and property of each disappearing party. At the same time, the surviving party becomes subject to all of the debts and liabilities of each disappearing party, and to any trust obligations resting on a disappearing party's property, in the same manner as if the surviving party had incurred those obligations itself. The statute separately preserves all rights of creditors and all liens and trusts on or arising from a constituent corporation's property, though a lien or trust obligation on a disappearing party's property remains limited to the property it affected immediately before the merger's effective date.

citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, succession to rights, property, debts, and liabilities on merger
citations.quote: Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existences of the disappearing parties to the merger cease and the surviving party to the merger shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing parties to the merger and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each and trust obligations upon the property of a disappearing party in the same manner as if incurred by the surviving party to the merger.

citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, preservation of creditors' rights, liens, and trusts
citations.quote: All rights of creditors and all liens and trusts upon or arising from the property of each of the constituent corporations and other parties to the merger shall be preserved unimpaired, provided that the liens and trust obligations upon property of a disappearing party shall be limited to the property affected thereby immediately prior to the time the merger is effective.

expectedJSON.gap: This section does not itself define what makes property subject to a "trust obligation" for these purposes — that determination (for example, whether a donor-restricted or dedicated-purpose asset is impressed with such an obligation) depends on separate California charitable-trust and cy pres doctrine that this document does not address. This document also does not quote subdivision (c) of this section, which addresses pending litigation continuing against the surviving party; the raw fetched HTML contains a stray double space at one point in that subdivision ("the surviving  party"), confirmed identical across two independent fetches on 2026-09-08, and this document omits a direct quotation of that subdivision rather than reproduce the anomaly.

The undersigned record, for Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust, that the board of each constituent corporation approved the agreement of merger on September 5, 2026, and that the members (or other persons whose approval was required) approved the agreement's principal terms on September 10, 2026 as follows: approved by unanimous written consent of the members entitled to vote.

If notice to the California Attorney General was required under Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(b), that notice, together with a copy of the proposed agreement of merger, was provided on August 10, 2026.

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: September 12, 2026

Jordan Lee, President

[This record describes the merger procedure that applies to a California nonprofit public benefit corporation under Cal. Corp. Code §§ 6010-6022. It does not itself effect the merger of Acme Community Fund and Beta Community Trust into Acme Community Fund or any other entity, is not the Secretary of State's official filing of the agreement of merger or the officers' certificate required by Cal. Corp. Code § 6014, and does not determine whether the Attorney General's consent is required for this particular merger. The current official forms and instructions are published by the California Secretary of State and the California Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts.]
